Bramwell Tallow.narrative: I keep the rope, tar and nail stall on the quay, and every fisher from the harbour mouth to the outer shoals owes me something or buys from me sooner or later. I came up hauling lines and I know what a boat needs before her owner does. The marks come slow in winter and the Kettlebridge nails come dear, but I pay my debts and I expect mine paid. Lately I have had to say so louder than I like.
values: keep the stall stocked before the purse
the quay looks after its own
goals: get the rope and tar money out of Wick Gull and Orvin Hollis
clear what I owe Josiah Crane for the iron nails before the next load
see Sella settled with a man who can keep her
keep the stall's name good with every fisher on the quay
teach himself to splice a proper long splice so he never has to buy one in
take a day to see the light on the north cape for himself, just once

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows the price of everything and I would be lost at the stall without her.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick and willing, but she has her eye on the fish road and I want her settled here.

relations.name: Josiah Crane
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He sells me iron nails and I owe him for the last load; he never lets a mark rest.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: A loud man with a good tongue and an empty purse; two tides now he has owed me for rope and tar.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: A good woodcutter and I like him, but a season of rope and tar is a season of marks.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent lad, but a crewman with a net to buy is not yet a household.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His cart brings the stone and takes my marks; the gate-due at Brackenford is robbery on both of us.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: warden
relations.note: She speaks for the quay and I pay her stall fee; she has enough on her plate with the seawall.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her noodle stall is two along from mine and she buys my lamp oil by the barrel.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: Orvin's good for the rope money and she's the one who'd see it paid; she keeps the Sootwood plots and trades roots at the stalls, so we talk plain enough.

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: debtor's wife
relations.note: Nia cooks the night crews and pays what she can, but she's not the one who took the rope, and I'll not shame her at the stalls for her husband's slack.

memories.gist: The night the surge came I hauled my tar barrels up the steps two at a time and still lost half of them to the water.
I bought my first load of iron nails from Josiah Crane on credit and paid it back inside a season; he has trusted my word since, but he still counts it.
Wick Gull took rope and tar off me before the last good catch and swore he would pay when the boats came in; the boats came in and he did not.
Sella was minding the stall alone when a deep-water man tried to talk her down on a coil of line; she held the price and he paid it.
I stood at the tide lanterns the night they read the list of the drowned, and my own name could have been on it if the surge had come an hour later.

stances.why: I have carried too many men's rope through a lean winter to let a debt slide.
Every load of nails I buy comes through Brackenford's gate and the due is added to my price.
The stall feeds us, but Sella's future is worth more than a season of marks.
The surge taught me that no stall stands alone when the water comes.
If the lower quay goes again, my stall goes with it.

pastimes: mending and tarring his own lines on the stall steps at first light
walking the outer quay to look over the boats and count who's out
a mug at the stall with Silas Pike, arguing over which rope holds best in a blow
Bramwell Tallow.calling: I know what a boat needs before her owner does, and I mean to keep the quay supplied till I'm too old to haul.

Perrin Tallow.narrative: I keep the pie and eel stall beside Bramwell's, and I know the price of every fish and every coil of rope on this quay. The marks live in my apron and I can tell you to the penny what we have and what we owe. Bramwell frets over the debts owed to us; I fret over my girl, who looks at a crewman the way I once looked at a man with a stall. I feed half the quay and hear the other half.
values: feed people well and they will come back
a household's marks are its own business
let the girl choose, but see she is kept
goals: get the stall's marks back from the debts owed to us
see Sella courted by someone who can keep her, without breaking her heart
keep the pie and eel stall the best on the quay
put by enough for the winter when the boats lie up
get her eel recipe written down properly so it isn't lost
put by a winter purse without Bramwell knowing the size of it

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a heavy purse-hand; I keep the marks because he would lend them all away.

relations.name: Sella Tallow
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: I see how she looks at Ostrander Mackerel, and I remember looking so myself.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A quiet, decent boy; he buys a pie and eats it slow, and he is kind to Sella.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We swap eels for noodles and gossip, and she has fed my family on credit more than once.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: He eats well enough at Nia's stall to pay something on the rope.

relations.name: Nia Gull
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A hard worker at the night stall; I would not have her man's debts laid at her door.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: She set my wrist when I fell on the steps and charged me a pie for it.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: runner
relations.note: She brings the Kettlebridge news and my girl admires her; I would see Sella on that road only with a good man beside her.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His timber comes down and my eels go up. A season of rope isn't worth a quarrel with him.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He sells salt and dried goods two stalls over and undercuts my eels with his cart. A fair trader, mind, but I count my marks twice when he's in the market.

relations.name: Dory Sedge
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her smoke shed's behind the market and her fish comes out sweet. We keep to our own stalls and that suits us both.

relations.name: Lyss Fenner
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her soup and bread at the tide steps catches the early boats before they reach my pies. We send each other what's left at the end of the morning.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She sells me lamp oil and dried fish for my stall, and she's right that the tide lanterns go up too late. I tell her so when the watch comes round.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her roots and eggs come down from Sootwood to my stall, and I send charcoal money back up the wood road with her man. A steady woman, though I wish she'd not talk so loud of the seawall never being built where my Sella can hear it.

memories.gist: The surge took the lower quay and the stall of a woman I had traded with for years; I fed the survivors from my own pot that night.
Sella was small and stood on a crate to reach the counter, and she sold a whole tray of pies before I came back from the fish market.
Bramwell came courting with a coil of good line under his arm instead of flowers, and I knew then he was the man for me.
I counted the marks in my apron after a good market day and found we were short; Bramwell had lent them to a fisher who never came back to pay.
Ostrander Mackerel bought two pies and gave one to Sella, and I pretended not to see it.

stances.why: On this quay a woman who cannot count her marks is cheated by noon.
The stall has fed half the quay on credit and they remember it when the boats are in.
I would not have my daughter married off by her father's measure of a man's purse.
What a household has is its own business, and I mean to keep ours.
I have cooked for the men who patch the lower quay with salvage, and salvage will not hold another surge.

pastimes: baking pies before dawn with the harbour noise coming up through the boards
trading gossip with Nia Gull over the stall rail
keeping a little book of prices and what each household owes
Perrin Tallow.calling: I feed half the quay and hear the other half, and I'd not trade my stall for any work on the island.

Sella Tallow.narrative: I mind my father's stall when my mother is cooking, and I can tell a good coil of line from a bad one by the feel of it. I like the quiet of the stall and the noise of the quay both, and I want to see the fish road before I settle to anything. Ostrander Mackerel buys a pie most days and eats it slow, and my father watches him do it.
values: hold the price and never be cheated
the road is out there and I mean to see it
family first, but a girl has her own eyes
goals: learn the fish road and see Kettlebridge with my own eyes
keep the stall's name good while my mother cooks
make my own mind up about Ostrander Mackerel
walk the fish road to Kettlebridge and back with her own eyes on it
learn to cook her mother's eel pies so the stall never wants for her

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: father
relations.note: He measures every man by his marks, and I wish he would measure Ostrander by something else.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She sees more than she says, and she has not spoken against Ostrander yet.

relations.name: Ostrander Mackerel
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He is quiet and kind and he does not talk over me like the deep-water men do.

relations.name: Juno Reyes
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She has walked the fish road and comes back with the Kettlebridge news; I would go with her tomorrow.

relations.name: Wick Cormorant
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He fishes with his father and wants a boat of his own, and he is good company at the stalls.

relations.name: Tam Harrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He runs errands for my father and knows every bit of gossip on the night market.

relations.name: Wick Gull
relations.label: debtor's family
relations.note: Father says his name loudly now. I serve him his eel and say nothing.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her stall's by ours and she always asks after Mother. She's kind and she knows everything.

relations.name: Sable Harrow
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: She keeps the oil and salt stall by the night market and counts every mark twice. Mother says she's sharp; I think she's just had to be.

memories.gist: I held the stall alone during a squall and sold a whole coil of line to a deep-water man at my father's price.
The night of the tide lanterns I stood with my mother and watched the names of the drowned read out, and I was glad ours were not among them.
Ostrander Mackerel brought me a pie he had bought from my own mother's stall, and we laughed about it on the steps.
Juno Reyes came back up the fish road with stone dust on her boots and told me what Kettlebridge's clock tower looks like, and I have wanted to see it since.

stances.why: I have heard the road described all my life and I mean to walk it myself.
My father taught me that a stall that haggles is a stall that starves.
My father measures Ostrander by his purse, and I think that is the wrong measure.
I want the road, but I would not leave my mother with the stall and the debts.

pastimes: feeling over coils of line to judge them, and testing herself against her father's eye
walking the quay at dusk with Juno Reyes, watching the tide lanterns lit
listening to the runners' talk of the fish road and the towns up it
Sella Tallow.calling: I want to see the fish road before I settle to a stall, and then perhaps keep one as well as my mother does.
